articles.headline: Tenderfeet vs. Cow Boys.
articles.text: In the Minneapolis Evening Journal of June 28 we notice an article headed "Rebellious Cow Boys." "The cow boys take possession of stock and refuse to yield control to the owners. Two captured and hanged and a stockman comes to St. Paul to see Gen. Terry to secure aid." This article was written on the information furnished by a Mr. Gallien, and is from beginning to end a lie, and the man Gallien a liar of the first water. In the first place Mr. Gallien never owned but 71 head of cattle and can hardly be counted as "a stockman." This tenderfoot Gallien gives the reporter of the Journal a fine sensational story for publication. The reporter, like a sucker, not only is gulled himself by the liar but gives the sensation to the public as truth, without ever taking the pains to make enquiry as to the responsibility of Mr. Gallien or the truth of his statements. Such a sensational yarn is calculated to work a great injustice to a good country, and an industrious and honest class of men—cow boys. It is only men possessed of but little sense and less experience, men who never traveled outside of their native township, who at the present day believe all the sensational stories told of cow boys. But the Bismarck Tribune and Governor Ordway are led to take stock in liar Gallien's statements, if we judge them by the statement contained in the Tribune of the 4th that Governor Ordway intended to order the Bismarck malitia to quell any future disturbance. This is just too ridiculous, and we advise his excellency to investigate such reports before committing himself in the public press. In a word there has been no disturbances or stock stealing by cow boys. On the contrary they are the first to assist in chasing stock thieves and bring them to justice, and if a man knows anything of the class called cow boys he cannot help but know that as a class they are honest, industrious and fearless; their life is one of hardship and adventure and calculated to remove the polish of civilization from their manners, but they are generous, hospital and extravagant to a fault and abhor a dishonorable action and dispise and hunt down stock thieves with vigor. If the malitia is not called into active service until it is necessary to take the field to fight the cow boys that organization we predict will never smell powder. In the future, Mr. Journal, ascertain the truth before publishing any such sensational stories, for to-day western Dakota is peopled with as law-abiding and peaceable citizens as Minneopolis or any old town in the New England states, and it is an outrage to publish such reports respecting any community without ascertaining first their reliability.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy calls the Minneapolis Evening Journal's 'Rebellious Cow Boys' story, based on a Mr. Gallien's information, a lie and chides the Bismarck Tribune and Governor Ordway for talk of calling out the Bismarck militia.

articles.headline: The Dakota Judges.
articles.text:
Frank Sperry who was nominated for assoicate justice of Dakota has declined, and the president nominated William H. Francis of Bismarck to that position. Francis is now receiver at the land office at Bismarck, and resigns to accept the justiceship. Mr. Sperry was at once appointed receiver at Bismarck and accepted the office.

Seward Smith, the nominee for associate justice of Dakota, is a native of Massachusetts, well educated, and has been in the law practice in Des Moines for twenty years. He is 53 years old. He was for several years a law partner of Generel Solicitor Withrow of the Rock Island road, and is justly regarded as a thorough lawyer, perhaps rather too amiable to shine brightly before a jury but hard to excel in drawing pleadings.
articles.summary: Territorial judicial appointments: Sperry declines, William H. Francis of Bismarck nominated; profile of nominee Seward Smith.

articles.text: A cyclone swept over the valley eight miles north of Deadwood at 4 o'clock last Friday, doing great damage. The track of the storm was about three-fourths of a mile in width and extended to a distance of four miles. Thunder and lightning, rain, hail, wind and the ugly funnel were characteristics not to be mistaken. Houses and outbuildings were swept from the face of the earth, fences wiped out, great fields of grain pounded deep into the ground, stock killed and maimed, in short the desolation was rendered complete. Several persons were seriously injured, and one, it is thought, fatally. The storm continued for about fifteen minutes.
articles.summary: A cyclone eight miles north of Deadwood destroyed buildings, crops and stock and injured several people.

articles.text: We find the following description of the cow boy going the rounds without any credit. It is the best one of many we have read: "The genuine cow boy is worth describing. In many respect he is a wonderful creature. He endures hardships that would take the lives out of most men, and is, therefore, a perfect type of physical manhood. He is the finest horseman in the world, and excels in all the rude sports of the field. He aims to be a dead shot, and universally is. Constantly during the herding season he rides seventy miles a day, and a majority of the year sleeps in the open air. His life in the saddle makes him worship his horse, and, with rifle and six-shooter, complete his happiness. Of vice in the ordinary sense he knows nothing. He is a rough, uncouth, brave and generous creature, who never lies or cheats. It is a mistake to imagine that they are a dangerous set. Any one is as safe with them as with any people in the world, unless he steals a horse or is hunting for a fight. In their eyes death is a mild punishment for horse stealing. Indeed it is the very highest crime known to the unwritten law of the ranch. Their life, habits, education and necessities breed this feeling in human life, and there are less murderers and cut-throats graduated from the cow boy than from among the better class of the east who come out here for venture or gain. They delight in appearing rougher than they are. To a tenderfoot, as they call an eastern man, they love to tell blood-curdling stories and impress him with the dangers on the frontier. But no man need get in a quarrel with them unless he seeks it, or gets harmed unless he seeks some crime. They often own an interest in the herd they are watching, and very frequently become owners of ranches. The slang of the range they always use to perfection, and in season or out of season. Unless you wish to insult them, never offer a cowboy pay for any little kindness he does you or for a share of his rude meal. If the changes that are coming to stock raising should take the cow boy from the ranch its most interesting features will be gone."
articles.summary: An uncredited sketch of 'the genuine cow boy' reprinted with approval as the best description the paper had read. (Region spans bottom of col 5, y 77-95, and top of col 6, y 15-29.)

articles.text: On the Tongue river round-up, west side, three buffalo calves were driven into camp with the cattle. One was secured by the boys, the other two got away.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Three buffalo calves were driven into camp on the Tongue river round-up (clipped from the Yellowstone Journal).

articles.text: An air saddle blanket or pad, is the invention of an Australian stockman, and it is spoken of in the highest terms of praise by those who have used it. We hope it may prove to be a preventative of sore backs.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Note on an Australian stockman's air saddle blanket (from the N. W. L. S. Journal).

articles.text: While from other localities we hear of crops and grass being scorched by the draught, we have had rain enough to insure a good crop, and the range is as fresh as it was in the spring, and we are losing fortunes by not having cattle to eat the grass that is free to all.
articles.summary: Uncredited note that ample rain has kept the range fresh while other localities are scorched by drought.

articles.text: One hundred and forty-six head of horses have been stolen this spring between Tussler's ranch and Billings. If the ranchmen would treat a few horse thieves to a hemp necktie, they might be able to break the business up in a great measure.—[Glendive (Mont.) Independent.
articles.summary: 146 horses stolen between Tussler's ranch and Billings this spring (from the Glendive Independent).

articles.text: Said Mr. Ratcliff: "I have raised side by side on the Divide, Shorthorn calves and Herefords—treated them just alike—and I will say to you now the Herefords beat the Shorthorns as rustlers all the time. As cattle for a high altitude the Herefords are fifty per cent. ahead.—[Colorado Record.
articles.summary: A Colorado breeder rates Herefords above Shorthorns as rustlers (from the Colorado Record).

articles.text: Round-up captains should be paid by the association. The duties of a round-up captain are many and of a most arduous character. Five dollars a day would be a very reasonable compensation for the responsible position, and we are sure that all association members who have been with the round-up parties this season will heartily concur with us in the opinion that captains should be paid.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Argument that round-up captains should be paid $5 a day by the association (from the New Mexico Stock Grower).

articles.text: Mr. Frewen, of Wyoming, the gentleman who has just returned from England, where he has been looking after the practicability of a northern route for cattle to Europe, gives it as his opinion that 50,000 head from Wyoming, Colorado and the northwest will this year take the northern route; travel through Canada, down the St. Lawrence, and finally as "feeders" land upon the coast of England, Ireland or Scotland.—[Denver News.
articles.summary: Moreton Frewen predicts 50,000 head will ship to Britain by a northern route through Canada (from the Denver News).

articles.text: Our advices from Ogalalla are to the effect that up to date there have been four herds of cattle passed. Two of these, six thousand, were for the Continental Cattle company, and have gone on to the north. J. R. Blocker has also had two herds of three thousand each to pass. These are early arrivals, and will reach their destination in the far north at a date much earlier than has been the case in past years.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Four trail herds have passed Ogallala, two of them for the Continental Cattle company (from the N. W. L. S. Journal).

articles.text: The most remarkable convention of the age will be the national cattle convention, which assembles in St. Louis in November next. More than two hundred millions of property will be represented in that convention. Not only will the cattle men of this country, but of the old world be present. Those who raise cattle on the plains will be supplemented by the breeders of choice stock to supply the wants of the growers of cattle. The widest circulation should be given of the proposed meeting, and the largest possible attendance secured.—[Coleman's Rural World.
articles.summary: Preview of the national cattle convention at St. Louis in November (from Coleman's Rural World). Region spans bottom of col 6 and top of col 7 (y 15-19).

articles.text: On behalf of the cattle ranchers of Montana the Canadian Pacific railway authorities have represented to the minister of customs the propriety of allowing cattle from the western states to be carried through the Canadian territory in bond for export. The Montana ranchers propose entering the stock at Fort Walsh; driving them to the Canadian Pacific railway for shipment. The effect would be to make Montreal the cattle market of Montana and other northwestern states. The ministry agreed to the relaxation of the custom regulations so as to bring this trade to Canadian ports.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Canada agrees to let Montana cattle pass in bond via Fort Walsh and the Canadian Pacific for export (from the New Mexico Stock Grower).

articles.text: The band of horse thieves who have been committing their depredations in the western portion of the territory were, we learn from the Madisonian Extra, arrested after a hot pursuit and sharp fight, by Ben Burns, Martin Peel, Deputy Sheriff Gloyd and a posse of citizens of Virginia City. One of the thieves named George Munn was killed in the fight. The names of the parties are Albert Edmundson, John Edmundson and Neil Murphy. John Edmundson was accompanied by his wife and two children. This whole band have been captured or killed and the horses they stole recovered.—[Billings (Mont.) Herald.
articles.summary: A Montana horse-thief band was captured near Virginia City, one thief killed (from the Billings Herald).

articles.text: T. A. Matthews, stock inspector of the Eastern Montana Association, whose headquarters are at Mandan, returned here this morning from a trip up the Missouri to Buford, Poplar River and Wolf Point. He states that he found the Assinnaboine Indians at Wolf Point in a very werk and sickly condition, so that they are dying off very fast. He attributes the mortality to the fact that they were nearly famished last winter and contracted consumption and kindred diseases that are taking them off now. Mr. Matthews recovered on the trip a couple of stolen horses. One belonged to Henry Tusler and the other was from the "T H connected" outfit of Wyoming.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Stock inspector T. A. Matthews reports Assiniboine people at Wolf Point dying of disease after a famine winter, and recovered two stolen horses (from the Yellowstone Journal).

articles.text: The Kansas Cow Boy says the Kansas Stock Association is raising $100,000 to buy the railroad land in the vicinity of Dodge city for the purpose of keeping the trail and range open, so that shippers can hold cattle and drive in to ship. Would it not be well for the Montana and Dakota associations to take time by the forelock and buy up the land at one or two points along the Northern Pacific road while it can be bought at a nominal figure and locate the government land in the immediate vicinity before settlers get too strong a hold? Already the railroad company is moving the stock yards at Dickinson to a point farther from the town, and business men of Miles City are making an effort to have the stock yards at that place located on the government reservation.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy urges Montana and Dakota stock associations to buy shipping-point land along the Northern Pacific, noting the Dickinson stock yards are being moved farther from town.

articles.text: At the annual meetings of leading cattle raising associations of Texas in 1882 prompt and very active measures were taken to banish the deadly six-shooter from the cattle man's belt. Resolutions were passed unanimously pledging owners of ranches and cattle not to keep in their employ any hands that would carry deadly weapons. That spring there was an absence of deadly encounters and shooting sprees observable throughout the range country. Last year no action was taken by stock men in convention assembled in regard to the "six-shooter," and since that time serious and deadly shots have been fired. In almost every section of the west murders are on the increase, and cow men are too often the principals in the encounters. The six-shooter loaded with deadly cartridges is a dangerous companion for any man, especially if he should unfortunately be primed with whisky. Cattle men should unite in aiding the enforcement of the law against the carrying of deadly weapons. Lawlessness in any form is hurtful, morally and from business standpoint, and no business is injured more than that of cattle raising when its employes are allowed to carry deadly weapons. Then we would suggest to the managers of cattle ranches to see that the six-shooter is banished from his outfit.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Plea for cattlemen to banish the six-shooter from their outfits (from the Texas Live Stock Journal).

articles.text: Mr. Cole, one of Montana's cattle kings, was down from Miles City yesterday and spent the day in town.
articles.summary: Montana cattleman Mr. Cole spent a day in town.

articles.text: The prospectors have all returned from an unsuccessful search for the precious in the Bad Lands north of here.

articles.text: The sheep shearing is progressing slowly on account of the frequent showers. There are about 200 to shear yet.
articles.summary: Frequent showers have slowed sheep shearing; about 200 remain.

articles.text: There was a very pleasant party at Smith's ranch, Beaver Creek, Sunday night, which was attended by some of the elite of Medora.
articles.summary: A party at Smith's ranch on Beaver Creek drew Medora society.

articles.text: If this number of the COW BOY seems a little thin or otherwise amiss we hope our readers will lay it to the inexperience of the editor pro tem.
articles.summary: The paper notes this number was produced by an editor pro tem.

articles.text: George Porter, manager of the company's store, received about a carload of household furniture this week and will occupy one of those elegant cottages.
articles.summary: George Porter, manager of the company's store, received a carload of furniture and will occupy one of the new cottages.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific Forwarding company shipped about 80,000 pounds of freight for the Black Hills this week, and have advices of considerable more which should be here this week.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific Forwarding company shipped about 80,000 pounds of freight to the Black Hills.

articles.text: Pete, the colored cook, had a narrow escape at the depot last evening. As the train was pulling out he attempted to jump on, but making a miscue he fell between the platform and the car steps. He hung on like a good fellow, and with the assistance of others he was pulled out without receiving any serious injury.
articles.summary: Pete, a cook, fell between platform and car steps at the depot and was pulled out unhurt.

articles.text: C. H. Du Bois, editor of Saturday Spectator and Midland Monthly of Minneapolis, and Prof. T. J. Richardson, artist, were here this week taking notes and making sketches for a series of illustrated articles on the Northern Pacific line. Pictures were taken here at the Cantonment, out on the Bad Lands and at the bend of the river above town.
articles.summary: A Minneapolis editor and an artist sketched the Cantonment and Bad Lands for illustrated Northern Pacific articles.

articles.text: Drawing room car No. 37 of the Pittsburgh, Cincinnati & St. Louis railroad passed through on train No. 1 Tuesday evening, containing about forty excursionists bound for the opening of the new National Park hotel. The party is from Dayton, Cincinnati and other Ohio cities. They expressed themselves as much surprised and pleased at the wild and weird scenery of the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: About forty Ohio excursionists bound for the new National Park hotel passed through Tuesday.

articles.text: A. T. Packard, editer and proprietor of the BAD LANDS COW BOY, and P. D. Cravath, correspondent of the Minneapolis Tribune, arrived here on Thursday evening direct from Medora. They were pleased with the country they passed over, and agreeably surprised with what they saw here. They went to Deadwood this morning and will return the first of the week to remain a day or two.—[Spearfish Register.
articles.summary: The Spearfish Register reported Packard and Minneapolis Tribune correspondent P. D. Cravath arrived at Spearfish from Medora and went on to Deadwood.

articles.text: The Fourth passed off very quietly in Medora. The day was generally observed as a holiday, but as no programme for celebrating had been decided on everyone passed the day as suited his or her notion, and, although several cow boys visited the town, each and every one behaved like gentlemen. In fact the place presented more the appearance of an eastern town in Sabbath garb than a western town in holiday attire. In the evening the new hall was formally opened with a grand ball, which was a decided success in every particular. There were about fifty couples present, and dancing was kept up till daylight dawned, and every one was unanimous in declaring the ball one of the pleasantest in their experience. Thanks to George Fitzgerald, of the Hotel de Mores, and his well-known and capable chef de cuisine, the old original Gen. Sheridan, the supper was like the ball a success and first-class in every feature. The hall was tastily decorated with flags and evergreens by Jimmy Hannigan, assisted by Joe Pennell, who are artists of no mean calibre whenever a thoroughly æsthetic display is called for.
articles.summary: A quiet Fourth in Medora ended with a grand ball opening the new hall, about fifty couples dancing till daylight.

articles.headline: More Horses Stolen.
articles.text:
Three horses were stolen from Sully Springs Sunday night. The picket ropes were cut.

About 10 o'clock the same night Geo. Roderick, at the Cantonment, on going to look after his horses found two men in among the herd, who made off as fast as possible on his approach.

About two hours later Pennell & Jones' herder discovered a man among his horses, who when accosted said he was looking for the brickyard horses, but on advice left forthwith.
articles.summary: Three horses were stolen at Sully Springs Sunday night, and prowlers were driven off from herds at the Cantonment and at Pennell & Jones'.

articles.headline: Freight Route.
articles.text:
Joe Pennell received the following telegrams dated St. Paul, July 5:

Rates only apply to Medora. Come and see me directly.
MARQUIS DE MORES.

Everything lovely. See Marquis' telegram and Pioneer Press. Belfield combination knocked out in one round.
KERR.

Later the Marquis writes that they will give stage and transporation contract rates, and are offering special inducements to a company to stock the line.
articles.summary: Telegrams from the Marquis de Morès and Kerr told Joe Pennell that Black Hills freight rates would apply only to Medora, beating a Belfield rival, and the Marquis offered contract rates for a stage line.

articles.headline: Little Missouri Round-Up.
articles.text:
Tom Smith, one of Clark & Plum's men, is in from the head of Little Missouri and Boxelder round-up.

This round-up commenced on the head of Boxelder, worked down as far as Stoneville, then leaving part of the men to hold the cattle they went to the head of the Little Missouri and worked down to Stoneville, where the round-up broke up on July 1. The weather was pleasant continually, and, with the exception of two accidents, was very successful.

Theo. Weedon's cook while bathing in the river undertook to dive from the bank and, the water being shallow, his head struck the bottom, nearly breaking his neck and paralyzing him for life. He was taken to Spearfish.

John Leahy, one of the "E6" men, was thrown from his horse, the animal falling on him dislocated his shoulder. He has fully recovered.

The boys roped two bear cubs and brought them to camp. They furnished amusement for many a lonely hour, but 'twas death to the bears.
articles.summary: Report of the Little Missouri and Boxelder round-up, which ended at Stoneville on July 1, with two accidents and two roped bear cubs. (Region: col 1 y 89-94, col 2 y 3.5-18.5.)

articles.headline: BELFIELD JOTTINGS.
articles.text:
The farmer's goose, thanks to the abundance of rain, hangs altitudelum.

Rev. Fulton is progressing nicely with a pretty new cottage located in Belfield's most romantic spot.

John R. Thayer has left for the east, and many expect to see him return with a wife.

Belfield is all broke up about the freight route. Men wear clean paper collars, women send for catalogues of hair pins and children frantically shriek for fire crackers in anticipation of it. Nobody knows anything about it, though everybody would bet his last 17th of March hat that the freight route is coming to Belfield. If so, look out for a boom with a big "B," and always remember that it is better to be born lucky than good looking.

Louis C. Hay, the only survivor of the townsite company, arrived home on Tuesday.

Several cases of burglary have come to light, the residences of the Galliens and McBirney being broken into and ransacked. A chain of evidence is fast closing upon the guilty parties, and as soon as all the returns are in they will receive their just punishment. People are tired of getting robbed, and the men implicated will be made an example of.

Quite a trade has sprung up in the bone business here. L. D. Pettit, of Deadwood, the prince of rustlers, who holds heavy contracts for bones, makes Belfield his headquarters, and what is better, pays over to ye hard-working bone pickers the solid cash at the rate of $8 per ton as fast as they can be delivered. In the language of the good old book, "Ye that have bones to pick, prepare to pick them now."

Bob Montgomery's neat addition looms up handsomely, and if Bob will only follow the example of others and take unto himself a partner as good looking as himself there would seem plenty of happiness and counterfeit half dollars in store for Bob.

New potatoes, fresh peas and other tropical vegetables are plentiful hereabouts for those who have the h. k.—hard cash.
articles.summary: Belfield correspondence: rain, new building, hopes for the freight route, burglaries at the Gallien and McBirney homes, and a bone-buying trade.
